common_name: Safrano Tea Rose (Classic Saffron-Orange Antique Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Safrano, introduced in 1839, is one of the oldest and most historically important tea roses, prized for pointed saffron-orange buds that fade to a paler apricot as they open.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. Safrano, introduced in France in 1839, is one of the oldest and most historically significant tea roses, its long, elegant, pointed buds opening a warm saffron-orange to apricot and fading paler as the loosely double flowers mature, carrying the classic fruity tea fragrance the class is named for. It flowers almost continuously from spring to frost and, like other old tea roses, shows good drought tolerance and resistance to blackspot in the humid Gulf South compared with modern hybrid teas, having long thrived in unattended Deep South homestead and cemetery plantings with little care. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood and control size.

common_name: Bon Silene Rose (Fragrant Deep Pink Antique Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Bon Silene, introduced in 1837, is a classic antique tea rose long grown in Southern gardens and cemeteries for its intense fragrance and reliable performance in poor soil.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. Bon Silene, introduced in France in 1837, bears deep rose-pink, pointed buds that open to loosely double, intensely fragrant flowers carrying one of the strongest scents of any antique tea rose, a quality that made it a favored cut flower and boutonniere rose in the 19th century. Like other old tea roses it flowers nearly continuously from spring to frost, tolerates poor, sandy, or infertile soil far better than modern hybrid teas, and shows good resistance to blackspot in humid climates. Long found thriving with no care around old Southern homesites and cemeteries, it needs only light pruning in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood and control size.

common_name: General Gallieni Rose (Dark Crimson Antique Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; General Gallieni is an antique tea rose notable for unusually dark crimson-red coloring, a color rarely found in the tea rose class, which is dominated by pastels and warm tones.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. General Gallieni bears deep crimson-red, loosely double blooms shaded with darker maroon tones, an unusually dark, saturated color for the tea rose class, which is more typically associated with pastel pinks, apricots, and creams. It carries the fruity tea fragrance typical of the class and flowers nearly continuously from spring to frost. Like other old tea roses it tolerates poor, sandy soil and Gulf South heat and humidity with good resistance to blackspot compared to modern hybrid teas, making it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for an heirloom rose collection. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Marie van Houtte Rose (Pale Yellow with Pink-Edged Antique Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Marie van Houtte, introduced in 1871, is a vigorous, large antique tea rose bearing pale yellow blooms edged in soft pink.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants generously to allow for its large, vigorous size. Marie van Houtte, introduced in France in 1871, bears large, loosely double blooms in pale creamy-yellow softly flushed and edged with pink, a delicate bicolor combination carrying the fruity fragrance typical of tea roses. It grows into a big, robust shrub, one of the larger tea roses commonly grown, and flowers nearly continuously from spring to frost. Like other old tea roses it tolerates poor, sandy soil and Gulf South heat and humidity with good resistance to blackspot compared to modern hybrid teas. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood and manage its size.
